summary: Proposes a method for splitting, recombining and sequencing datagrams across multiple logical data links, so several connections act like one faster one. It was replaced by RFC 1990.

eli5.summary: Cut a big message into pieces, send them over several roads at once, and put them back in order at the end.

subtitle: Bundling multiple connections into one faster virtual link

tldr.problem: Multiple simultaneous connections between systems offer more bandwidth, but sending packets across them requires coordination to prevent reordering and packet loss.
tldr.mechanism: Multilink splits large packets into fragments, sends them across multiple PPP links with sequence numbers, and reassembles them at the destination, keeping packets in order.
tldr.outcome: Several physical connections act as a single logical link with combined bandwidth, useful for ISDN and other multi-channel scenarios. RFC 1990 superseded it with improvements.

today: RFC 1717 defines PPP Multilink and is an Internet Standard. It was superseded by RFC 1990, which made improvements to the protocol.

sections.title: Why Multilink Works
sections.content:
When multiple data links connect two systems, bandwidth on demand becomes possible. ISDN offers multiple simultaneous channels, and async lines can back up leased links. The challenge is using these channels together without reordering packets.

The simplest approach—alternating packets between channels—fails because channels often carry packets in different orders. Multilink adds a small sequencing header to every fragment, so the receiver can reassemble them correctly.
sections.eli5: If you send pieces out of order, numbers on each piece tell the receiver how to put them back in the right order.

sections.title: How Multilink Works
sections.content:
Multilink is negotiated during the initial link setup using PPP Link Control Protocol (LCP) options. Once agreed, the sending system can fragment packets and send them across the bundle—the group of physical links treated as one logical link.

The bundle is named by the pair of system identifiers, which come from authentication and LCP negotiation. Each physical link can have different settings, but they all feed into the same protocol stack. Network protocols and their negotiation happen once on the bundle, not on each member link.
sections.eli5: Two systems agree upfront that they will use multiple roads together. Then they send and reassemble traffic as needed.

sections.title: Fragment Headers and Sequencing
sections.content:
Each fragment starts with a PPP multilink header containing a sequence number and two flag bits: Beginning (B) and Ending (E). The sequence number increments for every fragment sent on the bundle, regardless of which physical link carries it. By default, sequence numbers are 24 bits, but they can be negotiated down to 12 bits to save space.

The B bit marks the first fragment of a packet, and the E bit marks the last. A fragment can have both set if it is an entire unfragmented packet. The receiver tracks incoming sequence numbers on each link and detects lost fragments when the minimum sequence number across all links advances past an E-bit fragment without all intervening sequences received.
sections.eli5: Each piece has a number and tags saying if it starts or ends a message. If piece 5 is missing, the receiver knows when piece 6 arrives.

sections.title: Setting Up Multilink
sections.content:
Multilink is enabled by sending an LCP option during link negotiation. The Multilink MRRU (Maximum Receive Reconstructed Unit) option tells the peer the largest packet the system can reassemble, defaulting to 1600 bytes. The Short Sequence Number Header Format option lets peers agree to use 12-bit sequence numbers instead of 24-bit.

The Endpoint Discriminator option identifies the system sending the packet. It helps detect when two links belong to the same peer or to different peers. If the discriminator matches an existing link and authentication is present, the new link joins the same bundle; otherwise a new bundle starts. This is crucial when multiple connections from the same peer arrive.
sections.eli5: Before using multilink, systems say what size packets they can handle and how to identify whether a new connection is from the same peer.

sections.title: Detecting and Handling Lost Fragments
sections.content:
The receiver keeps track of the minimum sequence number received across all member links. When a fragment bearing the E bit arrives, reassembly is complete only if all sequence numbers up to that fragment have been received. If the minimum advances past an incomplete packet's end fragment, that packet is lost and must be discarded.

To avoid long stalls when the final fragment is lost, senders should keep links active by sending null fragments (header only, no data) when a link would otherwise go idle. The receiver should implement a link idle timer. Buffer space requirements depend on the channel delays and rates; implementations should allocate space for the sum of slippage across all channels plus maximum fragment sizes, preferably doubled for safety.
sections.eli5: If a piece goes missing, the receiver realizes it by noticing pieces with higher numbers have already arrived. Empty keep-alive messages prevent the receiver from waiting forever.

fields.name: B,E,Reserved
fields.desc: B: Beginning bit (1 = first fragment). E: Ending bit (1 = last fragment). Reserved: 6 bits, set to zero.

fields.name: Sequence Number (high)
fields.desc: High 8 bits of the 24-bit sequence number.

fields.name: Sequence Number (low)
fields.desc: Low 16 bits of the sequence number, incremented for every fragment sent on the bundle.
